Conclusion NMS reported higher negative mental health states than MS. Higher eHealth literacy was significantly correlated with higher negative mental health states in MS but not significant in NMS. Higher social capital was linked to lower negative mental health states among the MS and NMS. eHealth literacy in both MS and NMS showed a significant positive correlation with social capital.

title: Social Capital and Vulnerability as Determinants of Social Resources in Community Resilience and Crisis Management: A Cross-Sectional Survey of Riyadh Residents, Saudi Arabia
authors: MohseN Alattas; Saad Alkhurayyif; Mohammed Alkhurayyif
abstract: Understanding community resilience remains a persistent challenge, particularly in Arabian Gulf cities such as Riyadh, which is characterized by diverse social ties among various Saudi tribes. Dramatic population growth, immigration, and the influx of tribal groups to the city have transformed the economy. However, it has also increased vulnerability to a range of natural and health crises. This study investigates the role of bonding and bridging social capital and examines the social vulnerability indicators that are associated with the sub-dimension of social resources in relation to community resilience among residents of Riyadh during the crises. It applies a theoretical framework that combines social capital theory and Cutter et al.’s social vulnerability approach. These theories allow for a comprehensive assessment of social resources and classes of community vulnerability. Using data from a survey of 405 participants across five neighborhood sectors in Riyadh, the study empirically shows that social capital (bonding and bridging) is associated with the dimension of social resources in relation to community resilience. There was evidence of different levels of community resilience across vulnerability indicators. From A sustainability perspective, the finding highlights the importance of strengthening social capital and reducing social vulnerability as key ways to build resilient, sustainable urban communities that can cope with, recover from, and adapt to future crises. The study recommends that policymakers in Saudi Arabia’s emergency and crisis management stress strengthening social capital and address community vulnerability to enhance resilience and support recovery from future crises.

title: PENGARUH MODAL MANUSIA (HUMAN CAPITAL) DAN MODAL SOSIAL (SOCIAL CAPITAL) TERHADAP AKSES KEUANGAN UMKM DI KABUPATEN BINTAN
authors: Meysika Hesty Putri; Prima Aprilyani Rambe; Ronia Tambunan
venue: Business and Journal of Behavioral Economics (BJBE)
abstract: This research aims to analyze the influence of human capital and social capital on MSME financial access in Bintan Regency. The method used in this research is quantitative with data obtained from questionnaires distributed online via google form. The sample in this study was obtained using the purposive sampling method with the category of sectors or types of trade and industry businesses with a sample of 84 MSME actors in Bintan Regency. The data analysis method used is multiple linear regression analysis. The results of this study indicate that human capital separately affects MSME financial access, then social capital separately affects MSME financial access. Simultaneously, human capital and social capital together affect MSME financial access. The results of the determination coefficient test show that the independent variable is able to explain the dependent variable by 87.6%, while the remaining 12.4% is explained by other variables not explained in this research.

title: Social capital and diabetes care: a cross-country analysis of prevalence, diagnosis and glycaemic control in 11 European countries using SHARE data
authors: Laura Ceurvels; Jorik Vergauwen; Edwin Wouters
abstract: BACKGROUND: Diabetes is a major health issue that is increasingly prevalent in Europe. Providing high-quality care is crucial, as failing to do so can lead to various complications. This study employed a cascade-of-care approach and data from 11 European countries to identify the points at which patients disengage from the diabetes care continuum, and explored the relationship with social capital variables, sociodemographic factors, and health indicators. METHODS: Using cross-country data from Wave 6 and its related dried blood spot sample of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe, multilevel logistic regression models were constructed using a stepwise approach. The stages of the cascade of care were outcome variables: prevalence of diabetes, receiving a diabetes diagnosis, and achieving glycaemic control based on HbA1c levels. RESULTS: Higher levels of bridging social capital are associated with lower diabetes prevalence, partly mediated by sociodemographic factors and health indicators. Diabetes is more commonly diagnosed in older individuals (although this link weakens in the oldest age groups), men, and those in poorer health. Better HbA1c control is associated with having a partner in the household, lower BMI, and being a woman. CONCLUSION: This study highlights that social capital is associated with diabetes care among older adults in Europe. Bridging social capital can reduce prevalence, and having a partner can enhance diabetes control. Social capital also appears to be indirectly related to receiving a diagnosis. This reinforces the need for a combined medical and social approach to diabetes care.

title: Social Capital, Long-Term Care Insurance, and Older Adults’ Mental Health: Policy Spillovers and Implications for Gerontological Social Work in China
authors: M Li
abstract: Using 2015 and 2018 China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study data and a two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences design, this study examines how China's Long-Term Care Insurance (LTCI) affects the mental health of older adults who are not directly insured. Among 1,899 non-beneficiaries in pilot and non-pilot cities, LTCI improved health-related quality-of-life trajectories, with stronger spillovers for mental than physical health. Pilot-city residents reported greater vitality, social functioning, and fewer role-emotional limitations, suggesting mediation through structural, cognitive, and relational social capital. These findings highlight LTCI reforms as opportunities for gerontological social workers to strengthen community networks, outreach, and psychosocial support.

title: Social Capital Configurations for High Sustainable Development Performance in Chinese Platform Enterprises: A Dynamic Qualitative Comparative Analysis of Balancing Flexibility and Controllability
authors: Yuxiang An; Wensong Zhang; Rui Zhang; Jiayuan Wang; Baolian Chen
abstract: In the volatility, uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity (VUCA) era, platform enterprises face the critical challenge of balancing flexibility and controllability to sustain competitive advantage. Existing studies have examined these two dimensions separately but offer limited insight into their synergistic mechanisms within complex adaptive ecosystems. Drawing on the structural, cognitive, and relational dimensions of social capital theory, with a particular emphasis on institutional-level collaborative social capital among platform enterprises and their supply-chain partners, this study employs dynamic fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to identify the configurational pathways through which Chinese platform enterprises achieve high sustainable development performance. Using panel data from Chinese A-share listed platform enterprises (2014–2024), we identify three equifinal configurational pathways sufficient for high sustainable development performance: (1) a cognitive-relational alliance-driven path, (2) a structural-relational hybrid synergy path, (3) a structural-cognitive flexible innovation path. Innovation value consensus emerges as a core condition across all pathways. These configurations are sufficient for platforms to exhibit flexible market responsiveness and strategic controllability under varying environmental conditions. The study advances social capital theory by demonstrating the multidimensional, synergistic, and context-sensitive nature of flexibility-controllability coupling in platform governance. It also provides managers with actionable insights for tailoring social capital investments to specific regional and strategic contexts.

title: The Impact of Social Capital on Condom Use at Last Sex Among Sexually Active Young People in Ghana: A Cross‐Sectional Study Design
authors: Mark Kwame Ananga; Emmanuel Abu Bonsra; Rosemary Kafui Agbefu; Paul Narh Doku; Joyce Komesuor
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Young people in Ghana face heightened risks of sexually transmitted infections and unintended pregnancies, yet condom use remains inconsistent despite widespread awareness of HIV prevention strategies. Social capital, defined as the resources and support accessed through social networks, has emerged as a potentially important factor influencing sexual and reproductive health behaviors among youth. However, the relationship between social capital and condom use among sexually active young people in Ghana is not well understood. Objective This study aimed to investigate the relationships between social capital variables and condom use at last sex among sexually active young people in Ghana. Method A cross‐sectional quantitative study design was conducted via a community‐based household survey among young people aged 15–24 years in the South Tongu district of Ghana. A multistage cluster sampling method was employed to sample 792 youth for the study. Data collection utilized well‐designed semi‐structured questionnaires. Analysis of the data was performed via STATA version 16. Results The study found that 68.6% of respondents reported using a condom at their last sexual encounter. Multivariate logistic regression shows that area of residence, marital status, and four dimensions of social capital were significantly associated with condom use at last sex. Strong networks of connection were associated with higher odds of condom use (AOR = 1.84; 95% CI: 1.20–2.82; p = 0.005), while High social inclusion was also associated with higher odds of condom use (AOR = 1.58; 95% CI: 1.01–2.48; p = 0.045). In contrast, high trust in people and institutions was associated with 30% lower odds of condom use (AOR = 0.70; 95% CI: 0.51–0.97; p = 0.033). In addition, high overall social capital was associated with higher odds of condom use at last sex (AOR = 1.40; 95% CI: 1.02–1.93; p = 0.039). Conclusion This study found a relatively high level of condom use at last sex among sexually active young people. Selected dimensions of social capital were significantly associated with condom use. Strong networks of connection, higher empowerment, and greater social inclusion, and higher overall social capital were associated with condom use, whereas higher trust in people and institutions was associated with lower odds. In support of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Target 3.7, which seeks to ensure universal access to sexual and reproductive healthcare services, interventions should strengthen youth empowerment and supportive social networks while improving access to appropriate sexual and reproductive health information and condom services among young people.

title: Socially Integrative Social Media Use and Subjective Well-Being Among Generation Z: The Mediating Roles of Bonding and Bridging Social Capital
authors: Yesha Tomar
venue: Journal of Intelligent Decision Making and Information Science
abstract: The rapid growth of social media platforms has significantly changed how Generation Z (born 1997-2012) interacts socially, prompting important questions about how digital communication affects psychological health and Subjective Well-Being (SWB). While research has explored general social media use and well-being, the specific ways in which socially integrative social media use (SISMU), intentional activities aimed at maintaining and strengthening relationships, affects SWB remain poorly understood. Research Problem: The literature shows mixed results regarding social media use and well-being, partly because it is often viewed as a single, uniform behaviour. Additionally, the mediating roles of social capital dimensions, such as bonding social capital (BSC) and bridging social capital (BRSC), which could connect SISMU to SWB, have received limited empirical attention, especially among Generation Z. Objective: This study examines how SISMU influences SWB among Generation Z, focusing on the mediating effects of BSC and BRSC. Methodology: A cross-sectional survey was conducted, gathering data from 512 Generation Z individuals aged 18–27 through convenience and snowball sampling. The survey used validated scales adapted from previous studies. Data analysis was performed with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS- SEM) using Smart PLS 4. 0. Key Findings: The results show that SISMU has a positive and significant impact on SWB (β = 0. 214, p <. .001), BSC (β = 0. 432, p <. .001), and BRSC (β = 0. 389, p <. .001). Both BSC (β = 0. 318, p <. .001) and BRSC (β = 0. 267, p <. .001) significantly predict SWB. Mediation analysis reveals that BSC and BRSC partially mediate the relationship between SISMU and SWB. Theoretical Contribution: The study advances Social Capital Theory and Uses and Gratifications Theory by showing that both BSC and BRSC serve as dual pathways that mediate the effect of socially engaging digital behaviour on well-being. Practical Implications: The findings provide practical insights for universities, mental health professionals, and social media platform developers aiming to create digital environments that promote well- being among young adults.

title: Capitalizing Social Networks in Midlife: Longitudinal Pathways Linking Bonding Social Capital, Social Support, Sense of Control, and Mental Well-Being
authors: Marianne Simons; Jennifer S. A. M. Reijnders; Annelie Klippel; Trijntje Völlink; Nele Jacobs
abstract: Abstract This longitudinal study examined bonding social capital (BSC) as a protective factor for mental well-being during midlife. It was hypothesized that BSC provides two key resources, social support (SS) and a sense of control (SoC), that support well-being during a life stage characterized by physical changes, multiple roles, and significant responsibilities. A sample of 214 Dutch adults (40–60 years, 73,8% female) completed three online surveys at six-month intervals, measuring BSC (PSCSE, Simons et al. Simons et al., Aging & Mental Health 24:2034–2042, 2020) at T1, perceived SS (MSPSS, Pederson et al., Pedersen et al., Psychosomatics 50:461–467, 2009) and SoC (PMS, Pearlin & Schooler, Pearlin and Schooler, Journal of Health and Social Behavior 19:2–21, 1978) at T2 and overall mental well-being, comprising psychological, social and emotional well-being (MHF-SF, Lamers et al. Lamers et al., Journal of Clinical Psychology 67:99–110, 2011) at T1 and T3. Parallel mediation analysis using structural equation modeling with covariates showed that BSC was positively associated with overall mental well-being one year later, fully mediated by SoC after controlling for initial well-being. BSC was also significantly positively associated with SS, but the effect of SS on later well-being was not significant. Separate mediation analysis for the well-being subdimensions yielded similar results. These findings indicate that while BSC is prospectively linked to both SoC and SS, only SoC appears to initiate processes that support well-being. The results also point to the possibility of a sequential mediation model in which SS precedes SoC. Importantly, not everyone has equal opportunities to build sufficient social capital, leaving some groups more vulnerable than others to challenges during midlife. Strengthening BSC and coaching individuals in utilizing their social relationships to increase their sense of control can therefore be beneficial. A strong social network and the ability to draw on it effectively may be a key factor in successfully navigating the demands of midlife, sustaining optimal mental health, and fostering continued personal development.

title: Analyzing the Relationship Between Social Isolation and Social Capital Among Young Adults in Korea : Exploring Policy Interventions for Restoring Social Network
authors: 신한대학교 사회복지학과 강사; Cheol-Ki Min
venue: The Journal of Next-generation Convergence Technology Association
abstract: 본 연구는 청년층의 사회적 고립 현상을 사회적 자본 이론의 관점에서 분석하고, 사회적 네트워크 회복을 위한 정책적 개입 방안을 탐색하는 데 목적이 있다. 이를 위해 전국 만 19~34세 청년 782명을 대상으로 횡단적 설문조사를 실시하고, 사회적 고립과 사회적 자본(네트워크, 신뢰, 호혜성) 간의 관계를 다중회귀분석과 매개분석 을 통해 검증하였다. 분석 결과, 청년의 약 26%가 사회적 고립 상태에 해당하였으며, 특히 미취업 및 1인 가구 청 년의 고립 수준이 유의하게 높게 나타났다. 사회적 네트워크와 사회적 신뢰는 고립감을 유의하게 감소시키는 핵심 요인으로 확인되었으며, 그중 네트워크의 영향력이 가장 강력하게 나타났다. 또한 미취업 상태는 사회적 네트워크 감소를 매개로 고립감을 증가시키는 부분매개 효과가 검증되었다. 이는 청년 고립 문제가 개인적 성향이 아닌 구 조적·관계적 요인과 밀접히 연관되어 있음을 보여준다. 따라서 청년 고립 해소를 위해서는 고용 지원과 함께 사회 적 관계망 회복을 위한 통합적 정책 개입이 병행되어야 함을 시사한다.

title: A cross-sectional multilevel study of bullying victimisation among adolescents: the role of body weight status and social capital across 38 countries
authors: Ajeng Nova Dumpratiwi; Wen‐Hsu Lin
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Given the disadvantages of bullying victimisation on adolescent health, this study evaluates how adolescent body weight status, as the main individual-level factor, and social capital, as an essential country-level factor, affect bullying victimisation among adolescents globally. METHODS: The Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) study 2017/2018 included 143,091 participants across 38 countries. It captures the main individual factor and the individual control factor. Adolescents were categorised as “Else (Thinness or Normal)” or “Overweight and Obese (OAO)” based on IOTF age- and gender-specific cut-off criteria. The 2015 Global Sustainable Competitiveness Index (GSCI) captured social capital at country-level, while the 2016 Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and the 2016 Global Gender Gap Index (GGI) served as country-level control variables. This study utilised a cross-sectional multilevel approach to address the study aims. RESULTS: OAO adolescents were significantly linked to an increased risk of bullying victimisation (OR = 1.17, 95% CI [1.13, 1.21], p < 0.01), consistent across male (OR = 1.17, 95% CI [1.12, 1.22], p < 0.01) and female adolescents (OR = 1.16, 95% CI [1.10, 1.23], p < 0.01). At the country level, higher social capital correlated with a reduced likelihood of being bullied (OR = 0.96, 95% CI [0.93, 0.99], p < 0.05). An important interaction between social capital and body weight status was noted (OR = 1.01, 95% CI [1.001, 1.01], p < 0.05). A statistically significant but substantively minimal cross-level interaction between body weight status and country social capital was identified, indicating low variation in the relationship across country contexts. CONCLUSION: Research demonstrates that bullying victimisation arises from individual vulnerabilities and overarching systemic factors. While social capital at the country-level typically provides protection, its efficacy in alleviating weight-related bullying differences is limited.

title: Social Capital, Indigenous Knowledge, and Institutional Integration for Climate Change Adaptation among Pastoral and Agropastoral Communities in Borana Zone, Southern Ethiopia
authors: Muleta Husein; Terefe Tolessa; Chala Dechassa
abstract: This study evaluates the role of indigenous knowledge, institutional integration, and social capital in climate change adaptation by pastoral and agropastoral livelihoods in the Borana zone. A multistage sampling method was employed to select the respondents within the study zone. Borana zone was purposively selected and then the zone was stratified into pastoral and agropastoral livelihoods. From these categories, two districts per livelihood activities were selected. Within the districts households were randomly selected. A mixed-methods that integrated household surveys, focus group discussions, key informant interviews, and social network analysis was used to address the objectives set. Data was collected through a household survey on 365 households. The collected data was analyzed using descriptive statistics, structural equation modelling, Tobit regression, and social network analysis. The findings revealed that social capital was the main factor for participating in indigenous institutions (97.5% of households). Similarly, herd mobility was the most widely adopted climate change adaptation strategy by 87.7% of the households. These were followed by indigenous weather forecasting (83.6%) and herd diversification (77.8%). Livestock ownership, household size, wealth status, and education positively influenced the Social Capital Index, whereas these factors negatively affected pastoralism. Structural equation modelling showed that indigenous knowledge significantly improved adaptation to climate change through both direct and indirect pathways along social capital and institutional integration. Social networks are shown by high clustering and high density of 0.74 and 0.68, respectively. Therefore, the result showed that incorporating indigenous knowledge in social networks needs partnerships, and institutional collaboration between formal governance systems and customary law that can strengthen resilience and adaptation to climate change.

title: Pengaruh Human Capital dan Social Capital terhadap Kinerja UKM Keris: Peran Mediasi Strategic Agility di Kabupaten Sumenep
authors: Alfi Hasaniyah; Nur Syakherul Habibi; Muhammad Yasır Zaın; Syaiful Yasir Zain; Dian Lestari
abstract: This study examines the transformation of SME performance in the keris craft industry in Aeng Tong-tong Village, Sumenep Regency, by analysing the roles of human capital, social capital, and strategic agility. The study is motivated by several challenges faced by keris-based small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), including limited human resource quality, weak managerial capability, restricted access to modern markets, and low adaptability to technological change. A quantitative explanatory research design was employed. The population comprised 600 keris SME entrepreneurs, with 152 respondents selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire measured on a five-point Likert scale and analysed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with AMOS. The results indicate that human capital and social capital positively and significantly influence strategic agility, yet neither variable directly affects SME performance. In contrast, strategic agility has a positive and significant impact on the performance of keris SMEs. Moreover, strategic agility functions as a mediating mechanism linking human capital and social capital to SME performance. These findings suggest that improving the performance of culturally based SMEs depends not only on strengthening organisational resources but also on the capability to respond rapidly and adaptively to changing business environments. The study contributes to the dynamic capabilities literature, highlighting strategic agility as a mechanism that transforms organisational resources into enhanced SME performance.

title: The double-edged sword effects of R&D employees' age diversity on ambidextrous innovation in high-tech firms: a social capital perspective
authors: Hanqiu Zhu; Fuqiang Zhao; Yun Chen
abstract: Purpose Integrating social identity theory and socioemotional selectivity theory, we investigate how age diversity among R&D employees affects ambidextrous innovation in high-tech firms through different types of social capital (i.e. bonding and bridging social capital). Further, we examine inclusive human resource management (IHRM) as a critical contingency between age diversity and social capital. Design/methodology/approach We conducted two independent studies to test our proposed model. A pilot study (N = 194) was designed to test the role of age diversity in predicting bonding and bridging social capital and the moderating effect of IHRM. A main study (N = 328) was conducted using a more expansive sample of high-tech firms through a multi-source, multi-wave design to test the entire model. Hierarchical regression analyses and the bootstrap method were used for hypothesis testing. Findings R&D employees' age diversity hinders exploitative and exploratory innovation through decreased bonding social capital, while fostering exploitative and exploratory innovation through increased bridging social capital. In addition, IHRM attenuates the detrimental impact of age diversity on bonding social capital and reinforces its beneficial effect on bridging social capital. Practical implications High-tech firms should adopt a dialectical approach to the mixed impacts of R&D employees' age diversity on ambidextrous innovation. Moreover, IHRM practices should be implemented to provide equal opportunities for different age groups to flourish. Originality/value This research identifies bonding social capital and bridging social capital as critical mechanisms linking R&D employees' age diversity to ambidextrous innovation and reveals the beneficial role of IHRM between age diversity and social capital.

title: Spatial Inequality, Community Social Capital, and Age-Differentiated Health Vulnerabilities Among the Elderly in South Korea: A Hierarchical Linear Modeling Approach
authors: Yoonjin Lee
abstract: Background/Objectives: South Korea became a super-aged society in 2024, and this demographic shift is unfolding alongside the depopulation of rural municipalities across the country. How spatial inequality and community social capital jointly relate to elderly health—and whether those relationships look different for younger versus older elderly—remains an open question. We investigated associations between two dimensions of community social capital (sense of belonging and neighbor communication), subjective perception of capital–provincial inequality, and self-rated health among Korean elderly, with separate analyses for the Young-Old (aged 60–69) and Old-Old (aged 70+). Methods: We used the 2024 Social Integration Survey from the Korea Institute of Public Administration (full sample N = 2588; elderly subsample N = 1020). Random intercept hierarchical linear models accounted for the nesting of individuals within 17 metropolitan cities and provinces. Stepwise models examined social capital antecedents, a healthcare satisfaction indirect association pathway, and the direct association of spatial inequality perception with health. The elderly subsample was stratified into Young-Old (N = 289) and Old-Old (N = 731). A mixed-effects ordered logistic regression with Liang–Zeger cluster-robust standard errors was estimated as a robustness check. Results: Sense of belonging was positively associated with subjective health among the elderly (B = 0.065, p < 0.05) as a net of rurality and socioeconomic controls. Perceived spatial inequality showed a negative association (B = −0.070, p < 0.05). The indirect association pathway through healthcare satisfaction was not supported (Sobel Z = −1.458, p = 0.144). Age-stratified models revealed a striking split: belonging was the dominant predictor for the Young-Old (B = 0.149, p < 0.01), while neighbor communication (B = 0.078, p < 0.05) and spatial inequality perception (B = −0.092, p < 0.01) were significant only among the Old-Old. The ordered logistic robustness check confirmed the negative association of perceived spatial inequality across all specifications. Conclusions: What predicts health in the younger elderly is not what predicts health in the older elderly. Korea’s Integrated Community Care Act, set for nationwide rollout in 2026, should account for this divergence—prioritizing psychological community attachment for the Young-Old and face-to-face social contact combined with regional equity for the Old-Old.

title: Leveraging sociological systems theory: integrating transformational leadership and social capital to enhance quality of care – an exploratory longitudinal study of German hospitals
authors: Arno Stöcker; Jeffrey Braithwaite; Ludwig Kuntz; Verena Maschke; Holger Pfaff
abstract: BACKGROUND: Numerous studies have examined ways to improve care quality and patient safety. Further progress could be achieved by leveraging underexplored sociological concepts. To date, transformational leadership and social capital have been examined primarily as isolated factors in healthcare research to explain variations in hospital care quality. Yet, these concepts have rarely been integrated into a broader theoretical framework. Drawing on Parsons' AGIL framework, we identified two key social prerequisites for effective healthcare organizations: goal attainment and integration. We hypothesized that hospitals meeting both criteria would deliver better care quality. METHODS: Using a 2008 survey of medical directors in German hospitals, we measured transformational leadership (as a proxy for goal attainment) and social capital (as a proxy for integration). Data were matched with quality metrics from nationwide reports (2012-2019) on quality irregularities and quality deficiencies. Hospitals were grouped into high and low categories for both factors using a median split, and longitudinal panel analyses were conducted on 508 hospitals. RESULTS: The combination of strong transformational leadership and high social capital was associated with significantly fewer quality irregularities, but not with quality deficiencies. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that hospital leadership should strategically strengthen both factors to improve organizational capacity for quality improvement. This synergy likely fosters goal-oriented collective action, particularly the collaborative efforts required to enhance care quality and patient safety. Additionally, we propose that applying sociological theory offers valuable insights into the social dynamics essential for maintaining and enhancing quality and safety in healthcare settings.

title: Employee-perceived social capital, management-led marketing innovation and financial target achievement: evidence from an Indonesian software and hardware distributor
authors: Haura Salsabila Althaf Sudrajat; Santika Wijaya; Sintya Putri Khairunnisa; Mochammad Fahlevi
venue: Journal of Participation and Employee Ownership
abstract: Purpose This study examines how employee-perceived internal social capital, external social capital, management-led marketing innovation, and competitive advantage are associated with perceived financial target achievement at PT ACA Pacific, an Indonesian software and hardware distributor. This study is motivated by the firm’s transition from predominantly offline sales to online and e-commerce-enabled channels for Kodak Alaris scanner products. Design/methodology/approach This study uses an exploratory single-company design. Primary data were collected through a census survey of 50 employees of PT ACA Pacific, while secondary sales information was used descriptively to contextualize the firm’s digital sales transition. The survey data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Given the single-firm setting and modest sample size, the results are interpreted as evidence of associations among employee perceptions within PT ACA Pacific, rather than as externally generalizable causal estimates. Findings The findings indicate that employees’ perceived internal and external social capital are positively associated with management-led marketing innovation. Marketing innovation is positively associated with perceived competitive advantage and has a weaker direct association with perceived financial target attainment. Perceived competitive advantage is also positively associated with perceived financial-target achievement. These findings suggest that information sharing, stakeholder relationships, and digital marketing initiatives may support employees’ perceptions of competitive and financial improvement, although the results should be interpreted cautiously because the model relies on perceptual data from one organization. Originality/value This study contributes exploratory evidence on how social capital and marketing innovation operate within a technology distribution firm undergoing digital channel transformation in an emerging market context. This study also clarifies the boundary conditions of single-company survey evidence by distinguishing employee-perceived financial target achievement from objective firm-level financial performance.

title: Empowering leadership and innovative job performance in micro and small enterprises: self-efficacy and knowledge sharing as sequential mediators and social capital as a moderator
authors: Xinning Pang; Rachadatip Uppathampracha; Zhang Lin
abstract: In the digital economy, Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) are important drivers of innovation, yet their innovative capacity is often constrained by limited resources, operational uncertainty, and weak formal support systems. Drawing on Path-Goal Theory, Social Cognitive Theory, Social Exchange Theory, and Social Capital Theory, this study develops an integrated framework to examine how Empowering Leadership is associated with employees’ Innovative Job Performance in Chinese MSEs. Data were collected from 403 knowledge workers across eastern, central, and western China and analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The findings show that Empowering Leadership is significantly positively associated with Innovative Job Performance. This relationship is partially mediated through a sequential psychology-to-behavior process in which Empowering Leadership is associated with higher levels of Self-Efficacy, which in turn is associated with greater Knowledge Sharing and ultimately with higher Innovative Job Performance. The results also indicate that Social Capital serves as an important boundary condition, such that the positive association between Knowledge Sharing and Innovative Job Performance is stronger in high-trust relational contexts. By linking leadership, psychological resources, collaborative knowledge processes, and relational conditions in a resource-constrained setting, this study contributes to research on innovation, entrepreneurship, and organizational complexity. It also offers practical implications for MSE owners seeking to strengthen employee innovation through empowering leadership, knowledge exchange, and relational support.

title: Sharia, Digital, and Financial Literacy in Action: Transforming Social Capital and Digital Finance into Micro-Enterprise Well-Being through Financial Behavior
authors: Dani Setiawan; Sulaeman Rahman Nidar; Cupian Cupian
abstract: The Indonesian digital economy has encouraged micro-business owners' use of Digital Financial Services (DFS). These services have been widely adopted, but these actors' financial behavior (FB) and well-being (FWB) have not improved. This study analyzes how DFS and SC affect FWB directly and indirectly FB. Financial Literacy (FL), Sharia Financial Literacy (SFL), and Digital Financial Literacy (DFL) moderate the link between DFS and SC with FB. The quantitative survey study targets 300 West Java micro-entrepreneurs. Data was obtained using structured questionnaires and analyzed using SEM-PLS. Both DFS and SC positively and dramatically affect FB and FWB. FB also boosts FWB and mediates DFS–FWB and SC–FWB interactions. Moreover, FL, SFL, and DFL amplify the impact of DFS on FB. In the association between SC and FB, FL and SFL function as important moderators, whereas DFL does not moderate this association. The findings indicate that enhancing the financial well-being of micro-entrepreneurs is affected by access to digital financial services and social resources, as well as the quality of their financial behavior and their level of literacy.

title: The Effects of Social Capital Perception in Running Crews on Continuous Participation Intention: The Mediating Effect of Self-Efficacy and the Moderating Effect of Social Criticism
authors: Jungwoo Ha; Hyomin Suh; Hark-Kwon Kim
abstract: 본 연구는 러닝크루 회원들의 지속적인 활동 의도에 사회적자본이 미치는 영향을 자기효능감의 매개 역할과 사회적 비판의 조절 효과에 중점을 두어 탐구하였다. 최근 사회적 비판과 같은 부정적 외부효과에 대한 인식이 확산됨에 따라, 본 연구는 이러한 요소를 연구 모델에 포함시켜 스포츠 관광 분야 내 상생 방안을 모색하고자 하였다. 2026년 3월, 활동 기간이 6개월 이상인 러닝크루 참가자들을 대상으로 설문조사를 실시하였으며, 총 378개의 유효 표본을 확보하였다. 수집된 데이터는 SPSS 29.0과 PROCESS Macro(Model5)를 활용하여 분석되었다. 본 연구의 실증분석 결과에 따르면, 첫째, 사회적 자본의 모든 차원이 지속적인 활동 의도에 유의미한 긍정적 영향을 미친 가운데, 인지적 자본의 영향력이 가장 두드러졌다. 둘째, 관계적 자본과 인지적 자본은 자기효능감을 매개로 지속적인 활동 의도에 긍정적으로 작용했으나, 구조적 자본은 유의한 매개 효과를 보이지 않았다. 셋째, 사회적 비판은 인지적 자본과 지속적인 활동 의도 사이의 긍정적 관계를 약화시키는 부정적 조절 효과를 나타냈다. 이러한 결과는 러닝크루 활동의 지속성 확보는 스포츠관광 및 로컬 관광 콘텐츠 운영의 유기적 결합을 위한 실질적 단서를 제공할 수 있음을 보여준다. 즉, 고부가 가치 스포츠 관광 생태계의 지속 가능한 확장을 위해서는 내부적 사회적 자본의 축적뿐 아니라, 외부의 비판적 여론을 관리하고 지역사회와 상생하는 전략 마련이 도움이 될 수 있다. 한편, 본 연구의 횡단면 설계적 한계와 사회적 비판 여론이 지닌 특유의 맥락 의존성을 고려하여, 향후 연구에서는 종단적 접근을 통한 인과관계 규명과 더불어 다양한 참여 환경을 반영한 후속적인 척도 정교화 작업이 수반되어야 할 것이다.

title: Association between cognitive social capital and saliva-related quality of life among head and neck cancer survivors: a cross-sectional study
authors: Alan Carvalho Daros; Jéssica Klöckner Knorst; Bruno Emmanuelli; João Alberto de Almeida Gonçalves; Raquel Pippi Antoniazzi; Kívia Linhares Ferrazzo
abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate the association between cognitive social capital and patient-reported saliva-related quality of life among head and neck cancer survivors. METHODS: This cross-sectional study included adults treated with curative intent for squamous cell carcinoma of the lip/oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx, or larynx at a referral hospital in southern Brazil. The outcome was patient-reported saliva-related quality of life, assessed using the saliva domain of the University of Washington Quality of Life questionnaire (UW-QOL); higher scores indicate better outcomes. Cognitive social capital was assessed using a brief three-item proxy index; participants were classified as scoring 3 (the maximum) or below 3. Hierarchical multiple linear regression estimated unstandardised coefficients (B) and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI), adjusting for education, tumour location, radiotherapy (yes vs. no), and time since treatment completion. Sensitivity analyses tested alternative operationalisations and adjustments. RESULTS: A total of 105 adults participated (response rate 84.7%). The mean UW-QOL saliva-domain score was 61.85 ± 33.90, and 18 participants (17.1%) scored below 3. In the fully adjusted model, a score below 3 was associated with poorer saliva-related quality of life (B = -18.53; 95% CI -33.85 to -3.21; p = 0.018); sensitivity analyses were consistent. CONCLUSION: In this exploratory study, lower scores on a three-item cognitive social capital proxy index were associated with poorer saliva-related quality of life among head and neck cancer survivors. Perceived social resources may be relevant to this burden, but these preliminary findings require confirmation in larger longitudinal studies.

title: Longitudinal Associations Among Workplace Social Capital, Career Calling and Work Engagement Among Nurses: A Three-Wave Cross-Lagged Panel Study
authors: Niuniu Sun; Yamei Liang; Yang Ni; 张瑞宏; Yu Xing; Fengsai Bie
abstract: Background/Objectives: Nurses experience substantial occupational challenges that may affect occupational well-being. Understanding longitudinal factors associated with occupational well-being is essential. This study examined the longitudinal associations among workplace social capital, career calling, and work engagement in nurses. Methods: A three-wave survey was conducted among 470 nurses recruited through convenience sampling from a single tertiary general hospital in China between March 2024 and March 2025. Workplace social capital, career calling, and work engagement were measured at six-month intervals using established self-report scales. Cross-lagged panel models were used to examine time-ordered associations and longitudinal indirect associations among the three variables, adjusting for covariates. Results: Workplace social capital, career calling, and work engagement showed temporal stability. Workplace social capital was prospectively associated with subsequent career calling and work engagement from T1 to T2 but not from T2 to T3. Career calling and work engagement showed significant longitudinal associations in both directions. Work engagement also showed longitudinal associations with later workplace social capital and career calling. Exploratory analyses identified several model-implied longitudinal indirect associations among workplace social capital, career calling, and work engagement over time. Conclusions: This study identified time-ordered longitudinal associations among workplace social capital, career calling and work engagement in nurses. Career calling and work engagement showed longitudinal associations in both directions, whereas workplace social capital was prospectively associated with subsequent career calling and work engagement mainly during the earlier interval. Because the traditional cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) does not distinguish within-person from between-person effects, these findings should be interpreted as longitudinal associations rather than evidence of causal or within-person reciprocal processes.

title: Personality traits, nutritional knowledge, and social capital as determinants of livelihood diversification under disaster risk: Evidence from livestock households in rural Indonesia
authors: Jaisy Aghniarahim Putritamara; Agus Eko Nugroho; Tina Sri Purwanti; Agussabti; Sitti Bulkis; David Ponka
abstract: Building resilience in rural livelihoods against disasters and climate change is a major global challenge. Most existing models of livelihood diversification and disaster adaptation focus mainly on structural and economic factors, with less attention to the household behavioral and psychological characteristics that shape adaptive decision making under repeated shocks. This study examines how personality traits mediate the relationships between nutritional knowledge, market integration, and social capital, and the livelihood diversification strategies of livestock-raising households. In doing so, it addresses a gap in disaster risk and rural development research, which rarely incorporates psychological traits into diversification models. The research focuses on livestock households in disaster-prone regions of Indonesia: Aceh, Nusa Tenggara Timur, and South Sulawesi. Using data from a cross-sectional survey of 602 such households (response rate ≈ 94%), the study applied Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to examine mediation and moderation relationships among structural, cognitive, and behavioral factors. The measurement model showed reliability and validity (CR ≥ 0.70; AVE ≥ 0.50 with all indicator loadings above 0.70). The results indicate that nutritional knowledge and social capital are positively associated with livelihood diversification, both directly and indirectly through personality traits. Market integration, by contrast, had no significant direct association with diversification but did operate indirectly through personality traits, showing the importance of behavioral pathways that connect structural opportunities to livelihood strategies. Among the structural model factors, personality traits showed the strongest direct association with diversification, which suggests that behavioral dispositions are important determinants of livelihood diversification. Farm size significantly moderated the relationship between personality traits and diversification, meaning that resilience strategies differ by operational scale. By incorporating psychological factors into diversification models, this study offers new empirical evidence that livelihood resilience arises from the interaction between external resources and internal behavioral capacities. These findings suggest the potential value of combined interventions that pair nutrition education with behavioral skill building, strengthen market participation alongside entrepreneurial and risk management skills, and tailor social capital efforts to differences in farm scale. This research contributes to disaster risk and rural development scholarship by proposing a behavioral structural framework that integrates psychological traits with nutrition knowledge, market integration, and social capital to explain livelihood diversification among climate-vulnerable agricultural households.

title: Data Vulnerability Dan Online Well-Being: Kajian Apco Framework Atas Privacy Concerns, Protective Actions, Dan Online Social Capital
authors: Saraswati Kartika Sari; Yolanda Masnita; Husna Leila Yusran
abstract: Penelitian ini berada pada ranah pemasaran digital dan perilaku konsumen dengan menitikberatkan pada hubungan antara data vulnerability, privacy concerns, privacy protection behaviours, online social capital, dan online well-being dalam kerangka APCO. Studi ini berangkat dari adanya ketidakkonsistenan temuan empiris mengenai pengaruh kerentanan data terhadap kesejahteraan daring, serta belum terjelaskannya secara memadai peran kekhawatiran privasi, modal sosial daring, dan perilaku perlindungan privasi yang bersifat reaktif maupun proaktif dalam hubungan tersebut. Untuk menjawab persoalan itu, penelitian ini mengembangkan model konseptual berbasis APCO dengan menempatkan online social capital sebagai variabel mediasi dan privacy protection behaviours sebagai mekanisme protektif. Model tersebut diuji secara empiris menggunakan Structural Equation Modeling (SEM-AMOS) terhadap 159 pengguna media sosial di Indonesia. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa data vulnerability berpengaruh positif dan signifikan terhadap privacy concerns, yang selanjutnya mendorong munculnya perilaku perlindungan privasi, baik reaktif maupun proaktif. Temuan juga memperlihatkan bahwa perlindungan privasi proaktif serta online social capital berpengaruh positif terhadap online well-being. Namun demikian, data vulnerability tidak terbukti menurunkan online social capital, dan online social capital juga tidak memediasi pengaruh negatif data vulnerability terhadap online well-being. Secara teoretis, penelitian ini memperkaya literatur mengenai kesejahteraan daring dan privasi digital dengan menunjukkan bahwa pengguna yang memiliki kecakapan digital mampu menjaga kesejahteraan daring melalui pengelolaan privasi yang terencana serta dukungan jejaring sosial online yang kuat. Selain itu, model penelitian terbukti memiliki tingkat kesesuaian yang memadai dengan instrumen yang valid dan reliabel, sehingga layak menjadi dasar bagi rekomendasi praktis.

title: The Structural Model of the Relationship Between Urban Spatial Justice and Citizens’ Quality of Life: The Mediating Roles of Social Capital and Place Satisfaction in Tabriz City
authors: Aref Monadi
venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
abstract: The present study aimed to examine the structural model of urban spatial justice and its impact on citizens’ quality of life, considering the mediating roles of social capital and place satisfaction in the metropolis of Tabriz. Spatial justice, defined as the balanced distribution of services, resources, and infrastructure among urban areas, plays a key role in enhancing welfare and quality of life. Based on theoretical foundations and empirical evidence, a conceptual model was developed in which spatial justice affects citizens’ quality of life both directly and indirectly through social capital and place satisfaction. The study was applied in terms of purpose and descriptive–survey in terms of method. The statistical population comprised citizens residing in the ten districts of Tabriz. Using proportional stratified sampling, 350 valid questionnaires were collected. The research instruments included standardized questionnaires measuring spatial justice, social capital, place satisfaction, and quality of life. The data were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) and path analysis in SmartPLS. The findings indicated that spatial justice had a positive significant effect on social capital, place satisfaction, and quality of life. Moreover, both mediating variables played a substantial role in improving quality of life. The results revealed that the equitable distribution of urban services and facilities leads to an overall enhancement in citizens’ quality of life by increasing satisfaction with one’s place of residence and strengthening social bonds. This study emphasizes the necessity of considering spatial justice in urban policy-making and sustainable urban planning. Keywords: social cohesion, service distribution, civic participation, sense of belonging, urban planning Introduction The primary objective of this study was to examine the structural model of the impact of Urban Spatial Justice on the Quality of Life (QoL) of citizens in the metropolis of Tabriz. Specifically, the research analyzed the mediating roles of Social Capital and Place Satisfaction in this relationship. Problem Statement: Rapid urbanization has led to spatial disparities and the concentration of facilities in specific urban sectors. This inequitable distribution has created a significant gap in the quality of life across various districts, a challenge previously documented in Tabriz. Variables and Relationships: Spatial Justice: Defined as the equitable distribution of resources, services, and infrastructure, it is a prerequisite for the sustainable improvement of QoL. Quality of Life: A multidimensional concept (comprising objective and subjective dimensions) whose enhancement is a core goal of urban policy. Social Capital (Mediator 1): Involves networks of relationships, mutual trust, and norms of cooperation. Spatial justice fosters trust and participation, thereby strengthening social capital and QoL. Place Satisfaction (Mediator 2): Citizens' evaluation of their living environment (e.g., access to services, green spaces, sense of belonging). It acts as a bridge between objective environmental conditions and subjective wellbeing. Conceptual Model: The study proposes a model where spatial justice affects QoL both directly and indirectly (through the enhancement of social capital and place satisfaction). Literature Review The theoretical foundation of this study is built upon the intersection of urban geography and social psychology. Urban Spatial Justice, a concept popularized by theorists like Edward Soja and David Harvey, argues that the organization of urban space is a fundamental expression of social justice. When urban resources-such as healthcare, parks, and transportation-are distributed inequitably, it leads to "spatial marginalization". Empirical studies (e.g., Xu & Zhang, 2023) suggest that this objective spatial inequality directly diminishes the subjective Quality of Life (QoL) by creating barriers to basic needs and increasing the cost of living for residents in neglected areas. The Mediating Mechanism of Social Capital. Social capital serves as the social "glue" of urban life. According to Nahapiet and Ghoshal (1998), it consists of three interrelated structural, relational, and cognitive dimensions. Spatial justice acts as a catalyst for social capital; when citizens perceive their environment as fair, their trust in institutions and neighbors increases. This trust facilitates social participation and mutual support, which are critical determinants of a high QoL. In contrast, spatial injustice generates perceptions of deprivation, leading to social erosion and isolation. Place Satisfaction as a Subjective Bridge Place satisfaction is the psychological outcome of the interaction between the individual and the physical environment. Drawing on Relph’s (1976) "Sense of Place ", satisfaction is not just about the presence of facilities, but the meaning and identity attached to them. Spatial justice ensures that the physical environment is conducive to human needs, which enhances place satisfaction. This satisfaction, in turn, functions as a powerful mediator, transforming objective spatial attributes into perceived life satisfaction. Methodology This is an applied study utilizing a descriptive-survey design with a structural correlation approach. Population and Sample: The target population included residents of the ten districts of Tabriz. Using the Cochran formula, a final valid sample of 350 participants was selected. Sampling Technique: A proportional stratified sampling method was employed based on district populations, with questionnaires distributed through simple random sampling in public spaces. Instruments: Four standardized questionnaires were utilized: Urban Spatial Justice (Naderi et al., 2021). Urban Quality of Life (Rezazadeh et al., 2018). Social Capital (Nahapiet & Ghoshal, 1998; Persian version by Sabbaghian et al., 2019). Place Satisfaction (Relph, 1976; Persian version by Mohammadi & Mousavi, 2017). Data Analysis: The data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) and path analysis via SmartPLS 4. Measurement model reliability (Cronbach’s Alpha, CR) and validity (AVE, Fornell-Larcker, and HTMT) were assessed. Result Demographics: The sample consisted of 52.6% female and 47.4% male participants. The largest age group (41.7%) was between 31 to 45 years old. Structural Model Fit: The overall fit indices were favorable (SRMR=0.04 and NFI=0.89). Explanatory Power (R2): The model explained 61% (substantial) of the variance in Quality of Life, 37% (moderate) in Social Capital, and 27% (moderate) in Place Satisfaction. Predictive Relevance (Q2): Positive Q2 values for all endogenous variables indicated adequate predictive power. Hypothesis Testing (Path Analysis): All direct paths were positive and statistically significant (p<.001). Spatial justice significantly impacted Social Capital (β=0.610), Place Satisfaction (β=0.518), and Quality of Life (β=0.405). Both mediating variables also have a positive significant effect on quality of life: social capital (β=0.523) and place satisfaction (β=0.489). Mediation Results: Both mediating roles were confirmed. The indirect path "Spatial Justice → Social Capital → QoL" (β=0.320) and the path "Spatial Justice → Place Satisfaction → QoL" (β=0.250) were significant. Notably, the total indirect effect of spatial justice on QoL (β=0.570) was stronger than its direct effect. Discussion Relationship Confirmation: The results validate that urban spatial justice (equitable service distribution) significantly enhances the quality of life for Tabriz residents both directly and indirectly. Direct Effect: Equitable distribution inherently improves citizen satisfaction, aligning with previous findings (e.g., Xu & Zhang, 2023) that link spatial inequality to urban dissatisfaction. Mediating Role of Social Capital: Fair distribution increases trust in urban management, encouraging social interaction and cooperation. Mediating Role of Place Satisfaction: Spatial justice improves perceptions of safety, accessibility, and aesthetics, which directly elevates overall QoL through a "sense of belonging." Conclusion: Spatial justice serves as an objective mechanism for achieving sustainable development. Its impact is maximized when it fosters social cohesion and strengthens the emotional bond between citizens and their environment.

title: Building sustainable competitive intelligence through gig workers: Social capital, proactive behaviour, and subjective well-being effects on job performance in China
authors: Jin Jiang; Yuxia Kong; Sid Suntrayuth
abstract: The rapid expansion of the gig economy in China has intensified competition among platform-based businesses, creating significant challenges in maintaining effective competitive intelligence and workforce performance. Despite increasing scholarly attention to gig work dynamics, limited research has explored how social and psychological factors jointly influence job performance, particularly through the mediating role of subjective well-being. Addressing this gap, the present study develops and empirically tests a structural model integrating Social Capital (SC), Proactive Behaviour (PB), Subjective Well-Being (SWB), and Job Performance (JP), examining both direct and indirect relationships. Data were collected from 265 gig workers engaged in ride-hailing, food delivery, and online freelance platforms using a structured questionnaire. Each construct was measured using four reflective indicators on a five-point Likert scale. The study employs Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) to assess the measurement and structural models. The findings reveal that Social Capital significantly influences Proactive Behaviour (β = 0.325, t = 7.850) and Subjective Well-Being (β = 0.367, t = 9.210). Furthermore, both Proactive Behaviour (β = 0.289, t = 6.540) and Subjective Well-Being (β = 0.598, t = 17.540) exert strong positive effects on Job Performance, with Subjective Well-Being emerging as a key mediating mechanism. The model demonstrates substantial explanatory power in predicting performance outcomes. This study contributes to the literature by integrating social and psychological dimensions within gig work research and offers practical implications for digital platform managers to enhance worker performance through fostering social connections, encouraging proactive engagement, and supporting well-being initiatives.

title: Social Capital, Life Meaning, and Depressive Symptoms Among Older Adults in China: The Moderating Roles of Digital Social Participation and Digital Social Interaction
authors: Jingfang Liu; Chengyang Fu; Dingyun Lou
abstract: Population aging and digitization are two defining trends in China, yet how digital forms of social participation and interaction condition the association between social capital and older adults’ mental health remains unclear. Using cross-sectional data from the 2022 China Family Panel Studies (N = 4394 adults aged 60 years and above), this study examined whether two bounded indicators of social capital—intergenerational interaction frequency and interpersonal trust—are associated with depressive symptoms, whether life meaning carries part of those associations, and whether two forms of digital social engagement moderate them. A moderated mediation model with five regression equations was estimated by survey-weighted least squares, with design-based standard errors and confidence intervals obtained by bootstrap replication of primary sampling units. Both intergenerational interaction frequency (β = −0.238, p < 0.001) and interpersonal trust (β = −0.756, p < 0.001) were negatively associated with depressive symptoms, and the indirect associations through life meaning were −0.047 (95% CI −0.072 to −0.021) and −0.163 (95% CI −0.252 to −0.074) respectively, accounting for 19.6% and 21.6% of the corresponding total associations. Both digital measures moderated associations within the model and in opposite directions: the negative association between interpersonal trust and depressive symptoms was stronger among respondents who used WeChat (interaction β = −0.719, p = 0.011), whereas the positive association between intergenerational interaction frequency and life meaning was weaker among those who shared more often on WeChat Moments (interaction β = −0.035, p < 0.001). These findings suggest that digital social participation and digital social interaction are not merely independent correlates of older adults’ mental health but conditions under which the associations between specific social capital indicators and mental health take different forms.

title: The effect of social capital on infectious disease-specific health literacy among community residents: the chain mediating effect of family health and psychological capital
authors: Huan Xu; Xixi Zhang; Qian Yang; Hanlu Du; Hongjuan Lang
abstract: Objective: This study aims to investigate how social capital affects infectious disease-specific health literacy among Chinese community residents, with a focus on the mediating roles of family health and psychological capital. The findings offer both theoretical insights and practical recommendations for enhancing infectious disease-specific health literacy among residents in a systematic manner. Methods: This cross-sectional study utilized convenience sampling to survey 415 residents from five communities in Xi'an, China, between September and October 2025. The survey collected data on sociodemographic characteristics, social capital, family health, psychological capital, and infectious disease health literacy. Data analysis was performed using SPSS 27.0 and AMOS 26.0. Results: = 0.329, accounting for 35.45% of the total effect) and also exerted indirect effects through both independent and chained mediations involving family health and psychological capital. Specifically, the independent mediating effect of family health accounted for 38.90% of the total effect, while the effect of psychological capital contributed 17.03%. The combined chained mediating effect of both factors accounted for 8.62%. All hypotheses were confirmed. Conclusion: Social capital directly influences residents' infectious disease-specific health literacy and indirectly affects it through the mediating pathways of family health and psychological capital. Therefore, implementing a comprehensive intervention strategy that "cultivates community social capital, optimizes family health functions, and enhances residents' psychological capital" provides an effective approach to systematically improving infectious disease-specific health literacy among community residents and strengthening grassroots epidemic prevention networks.

title: The Impact of Social Media on the Cross-Cultural Psychological Adaptation of African International Students in China: A Mediating Effect Study Based on Bonding Social Capital
authors: Li Kunruonan
abstract: Against the backdrop of the convergence of internationalization and digitalization in global higher education, how social media influences the psychological adaptation of international students has become an issue of both theoretical and practical significance. This study focuses on African international students in China. Moving beyond a unidimensional examination of social media "usage intensity," it introduces the dimension of "usage behavior" and explores the key mediating role of "bonding social capital." Through a questionnaire survey of 390 African students from universities in cities such as Guangzhou, Shanghai, and Nanjing, and employing hierarchical regression analysis and Bootstrap mediation tests, the study finds: First, both social media usage intensity and usage behavior can significantly and negatively predict cultural adaptation stress, with "usage behavior" demonstrating a stronger and more stable predictive effect. Second, bonding social capital plays a full mediating role, but its effect direction contradicts theoretical expectations. Specifically, active social media usage behavior, by enhancing the students' perceived strong ties with their original cultural circles (i.e., bonding social capital), exacerbates their cultural adaptation stress in the host country. This "double-edged sword" effect reveals that in a cross-cultural context, strong native ties reinforced by social media may evolve into a "psychological comfort zone" or "cultural echo chamber." While providing emotional support, they may also intensify cultural comparison, delay the adaptation process, and ultimately lead to greater psychological conflict. This study not only deepens the understanding of the complex mechanisms linking social media use and cross-cultural adaptation, revising the traditional assumption of the unidirectional positive effect of bonding social capital, but also provides empirical evidence and theoretical insights for Chinese universities to optimize social support and psychological services for international students and guide their rational use of social media.

title: Disclosure of green social capital and its impact on financial performance: An empirical study of green operations innovations according to management accounting procedures in Iraq
authors: Noor S Hazim
venue: International Journal of Financial Management and Economics
abstract: The research aims to study and analyze the concept of green social capital disclosure and its impact on the company’s financial performance, through discovering green process innovations according to management accounting procedures, which are defined as any decent job that contributes to maintaining the quality of the environment in various sectors, whether industrial or commercial, The reason for these processes is that the term green social capital is the basis of sustainable development, as sustainable development cannot occur in a society that suffers from a lack of harmony between its various social components, The research dealt with the analysis and interpretation of each variable through the use of content analysis of the annual financial statements of a sample of (12) banks listed on the Iraq Stock Exchange, for the period from (2012-2022). Correlation and regression models were used to examine the relationship and impact between these variables, The research concluded that there is an impact of disclosing green social capital on the financial performance of the banks in the research sample, and that this impact is negative. However, discovering green process innovations according to management accounting procedures as an interactive variable contributes effectively to enhancing the level of that negative impact. The results of the current research contribute to highlighting the reality of social capital of its various types in terms of whether it can be an added value and a competitive advantage for the company or not, or whether it leads to improving its financial performance and increasing its profits.

title: Pengaruh Social Capital Terhadap Minat Membayar Zakat Dengan Loyalitas sebagai Variabel Intervening di BAZNAS Provinsi Kepulauan Bangka Belitung
authors: Salwa Nabila Az Zahra; Peny Cahaya Azwari; Siti Mardiah
abstract: This study aims to determine the effect of social capital on the interest in paying zakat with loyalty as an intervening variable at BAZNAS of the Bangka Belitung Islands Province. The background of the study is the decreasing trend in zakat fund collection from IDR 12.63 billion (2020) to IDR 2.65 billion (2025), which indicates weak social capital and loyalty of muzakki. The quantitative research method with a sample of 96 muzakki from a population of 1,728 people, analyzed using SEM-PLS. The results of the study prove: (1) Social capital has a positive and significant effect on the interest in paying zakat; (2) Social capital has a positive and significant effect on loyalty; (3) Loyalty has a positive and significant effect on the interest in paying zakat; (4) Loyalty significantly mediates the effect of social capital on the interest in paying zakat. The R-square value of 0.709 indicates that the social capital and loyalty variables are able to explain the interest in paying zakat by 70.9%. Overall, strong social capital (trust, social networks, and norms) will build loyalty among zakat payers, which in turn increases their willingness to pay zakat. Loyalty plays a crucial role as a variable that strengthens the relationship between social capital and willingness to pay zakat.

title: Explaining Turnover Intention among Generation Z Contract Employees through Psychological, Physical, and Social Capital: Evidence from the Telecommunications BPO Industry
authors: Zihaul Haq; Puspita Wulansari
venue: International Journal of Indonesian Business Review
abstract: Purpose – Employee turnover has become a major human resource challenge in the telecommunications Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) industry, particularly among Generation Z contract employees. This study examines the effects of psychological capital, physical capital, and social capital on turnover intention, with job satisfaction as a mediating variable. Methodology/approach – A quantitative explanatory approach was employed using survey data collected from 338 Generation Z employees working under fixed-term employment contracts in the telecommunications division of BPO Company XYZ. Respondents were selected through purposive sampling. Structural Equation Modeling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS) with SmartPLS 4 was utilized to assess both direct and indirect relationships among the proposed constructs. Findings – The results indicate that psychological capital, physical capital, and social capital significantly enhance job satisfaction, with physical capital exerting the strongest effect. Job satisfaction significantly reduces turnover intention and mediates the relationships between all three forms of capital and turnover intention. The model explains 63.2% of the variance in job satisfaction and 51.5% of the variance in turnover intention. Descriptive findings further highlight career opportunity, trust, work facilities, optimism, and resilience as priority areas for improving employee retention. Novelty – This study contributes to the Human Resource Management and Organizational Behavior literature by proposing an integrated model that examines psychological, physical, and social capital simultaneously as antecedents of turnover intention through the mediating role of job satisfaction. It also provides empirical evidence from Generation Z contract employees in the telecommunications BPO industry, offering a more comprehensive perspective on employee retention strategies.

title: The Effect of Artificial Intelligence Competency on Life Satisfaction among Persons with Disabilities: The Mediating Effect of Economic Activity Participation and the Moderating Effect of Social Capital
authors: Mi-ran Joo; Jin-Won Kim; Eun-Hyung Lee
venue: Journal of the Korea Academia-Industrial cooperation Society
abstract: 본 연구는 장애인의 인공지능(AI) 역량이 삶의 만족도에 미치는 영향에서 경제활동 참여 수준의 매개효과와 사회적 자본의 조절효과를 검증하고자 하였다. AI 기술이 일상에 빠르게 확산되는 가운데, 장애인의 AI 역량이 삶의 질로 이어지는 구체적 경로와 조건을 규명하는 것은 디지털 포용 정책 설계에 중요한 함의를 가진다. 한국지능정보사회진흥원의 「2024년 디지털정보 격차 실태조사」 장애인 응답자 중 PC·모바일 기반 경제활동 참여 관련 문항에 응답한 1,918명을 분석 대상으로 하였으며, SPSS 21.0과 PROCESS Macro v4.2 Model 7을 적용하여 분석을 실시하였다. 주요 결과는 다음과 같다. 첫째, 인공지능 역량은 삶의 만족도에 유의한 정적 영향을 미쳤다(B=.197, p<.001). 둘째, 인공지능 역량이 경제활동 참여 수준을 매개로 삶의 만족도에 미치는 간접효과가 통계적으로 유의하였다. 셋째, 사회적 자본은 인공지능 역량과 경제활동 참여 수준의 관계를 정적으로 조절하였으며(B=.106, p<.001), 조절된 매개효과 지수도 유의하였다(Index=.017, 95% CI[.008, .028]). 즉, 사회적 자본이 높을수록 인공지능 역량이 경제활동 참여를 매개로 삶의 만족도에 미치는 간접효과가 점진적으로 증가하였다. 본 연구 결과는 장애인의 AI 역량 강화와 사회적 자본 형성을 동시에 지원하는 통합적 정책 접근이 필요함을 시사한다.

title: Negative Life Events and Psychological Distress Among Rural Chinese Older Adults with Hypertension: A Moderated Mediation Model of Self-Efficacy and Social Capital
authors: Yingjie Fu; Runqi Zhang; Shuo Zhang; Jiyao Sun; Xiaojie Sun; Yuanli Liu
abstract: Background: Although negative life events have been linked to poorer mental health among older adults, how self-efficacy and social capital jointly relate to this association remains unclear among older adults with hypertension, who face additional demands of chronic disease management. We examined the mediating role of self-efficacy and the moderating role of social capital in the association between negative life events and psychological distress. Methods: This cross-sectional survey included 953 rural older adults with hypertension in Shandong, China. Negative life events in the preceding 12 months were self-reported. Psychological distress, self-efficacy, and social capital were measured using the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K10), General Self-Efficacy Scale (GSES), and Resource Generator Scale for China (RG-China), respectively. Hierarchical multiple linear regression and PROCESS Models 4 and 15 assessed mediation and moderated mediation using 5000 bootstrap resamples. Results: Negative life events were positively associated with psychological distress (β = 0.418). The indirect association through self-efficacy was 0.053 (95% CI: 0.035–0.073), accounting for 12.7% of the total association. Higher social capital was associated with a weaker positive association between negative life events and psychological distress (interaction β = −0.058) and a weaker negative association between self-efficacy and psychological distress (interaction β = 0.059). The index of moderated mediation was −0.012 (95% bootstrap CI: −0.023 to −0.001). Conclusions: Self-efficacy accounted for part of the association between negative life events and psychological distress, while social capital moderates both the direct and indirect associations. Social capital may be an important consideration in developing and evaluating future strategies to support psychological well-being and hypertension management among vulnerable older adults.

title: Psychological distress, self-determination, and social capital associated with quality of life among retirees in Sarawak: a cross-sectional structural equation modelling analysis
authors: Sivanandhan Selleyitoreea; Md Mizanur Rahman
abstract: BACKGROUND: Population aging is accelerating in middle-income countries; however, evidence on the psychosocial factors associated with later-life quality of life (QoL) remains limited in Southeast Asian settings. Psychological distress, self-determination, and social capital have each been linked to well-being in older populations, but few studies have examined these constructs together among retirees in geographically dispersed, multiethnic populations. This study examined the associations between psychological distress, self-determination, social capital, catastrophic health expenditure (CHE), and QoL among retirees in Sarawak, Malaysia. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1,410 retirees aged 60 years and above across nine districts in southern, central, and northern Sarawak. QoL was measured using the WHOQOL-BREF; psychological distress using the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scales-21; self-determination through basic psychological need satisfaction comprising autonomy, competence, and relatedness; and social capital using bonding and bridging indicators. CHE was assessed using health-related out-of-pocket expenditure thresholds. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling with 10,000 bootstrap resamples examined direct associations, statistical mediation pathways, and moderation effects. Hierarchical multiple regression assessed incremental variance explained by sociodemographic, health-related, and psychosocial variables. RESULTS: The PLS-SEM model explained 56% of the variance in QoL. Self-determination showed the strongest positive association with QoL (β = 0.546, p < .001), followed by social capital (β = 0.352, p < .001). Psychological distress was negatively associated with self-determination (β = -0.379, p < .001) and social capital (β = -0.327, p < .001). Significant indirect associations were observed between psychological distress and QoL through self-determination (β = -0.207, 95% bootstrap confidence interval [BCa] CI: -0.233, -0.181) and social capital (β = -0.115, 95% BCa CI: -0.135, -0.097). CHE showed small, non-significant main direct and indirect associations with QoL. A small CHE by social capital interaction was observed for self-determination (β = -0.06, p = .013), requiring cautious interpretation. Hierarchical regression showed that health-related variables and CHE produced a large incremental increase in explained variance across Qol domains, while psychosocial variables added a further substantial 20-30%. CONCLUSIONS: In this cross-sectional sample, QoL was more strongly associated with psychological distress, self-determination, and social capital than with CHE. Self-determination appeared to be the strongest statistical pathway linking psychological distress with QoL. Healthy aging strategies may benefit from greater attention to mental health, autonomy, competence, relatedness, and social connectedness. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal relationships and causal mechanisms.

title: Life satisfaction among older migrants in urban Zhejiang: comparing the roles of family and community social capital across later-life migration pathways
authors: Wusi Zhou; Yixi Xu; Man Li; Xiangjing Zhang
abstract: Population ageing and internal migration have increased the number of older migrants, making life satisfaction (LS) an important population-level indicator of well-being in later life. LS among older migrants may be associated with changes in family and community ties after relocation. However, population-based evidence remains limited on whether and how family and community social capital are differently associated with LS across distinct later-life migration pathways. This study examines the associations between family and community social capital and LS among older migrants in urban Zhejiang, China, across three migration subgroups: quality-of-life-oriented (QLO), family-support (FS), and economically driven (ED) migrants. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1,216 older migrants in four major cities in Zhejiang Province, China, yielding 1,105 valid responses. Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was used to examine bivariate associations between LS and social capital indicators. Binary logistic regression models were estimated for the full sample and separately for QLO, FS, and ED migrants to assess the associations of family social capital, structural social capital (SSC), and cognitive social capital (CSC) with high LS. Pooled interaction models were further estimated to test for cross-group differences. Overall, 57.74% of respondents reported high LS, with a mean score of 3.66. LS varied across migration pathways, with the highest level observed among QLO migrants, followed by FS and ED migrants. In the full sample, co-residence with family members (OR = 2.416, p < 0.01), family relationship quality (OR = 1.231, p < 0.01) and satisfaction with living conditions (OR = 1.520, p < 0.001) were positively associated with high LS. Co-residence with family members was also significantly associated with high LS among ED migrants (OR = 3.430, p < 0.01), but this association was not significant across all subgroups. SSC showed limited and inconsistent associations with high LS in the multivariable models. In contrast, CSC indicators were more consistently associated with high LS, particularly perceived reciprocity, perceived community support, and sense of belonging. Pooled interaction models indicated that the association between perceived community support and high LS was stronger among ED migrants than among QLO migrants, while the corresponding difference between FS and QLO migrants was marginal. LS among older migrants differed across later-life migration pathways, and the associations of family and community social capital with LS varied across subgroups. Compared with SSC, CSC showed more consistent associations with LS, suggesting that subjective relational integration may be more closely associated with LS than formal participation after later-life migration. These findings highlight the need for pathway-sensitive interventions that strengthen both family-based support and migrants’ perceived integration into urban communities.
