A large-scale survey of 503 respondents supports these findings and provides insights to guide future research into volunteer motivations. This study contributes to the Humanitarian Operations Management literature and informs the strategies of NGOs regarding religious alignments, volunteer recruitment and retention, and operational performance.

title: Retention and attrition of community health volunteers in rural Malawi; a mixed-methods study
authors: Blessings Nyasilia Kaunda-Khangamwa; Harrison Msuku; Cecilia T. Kamiza; Alfred A. Chimala; Christopher C. Stanley; Jobiba Chinkhumba
abstract: BACKGROUND: Community health volunteers (CHVs) are an important resource for supporting health service delivery, surveillance, and social programmes. However, retention and attrition of CHVs remain a big challenge. This study explored factors affecting the retention and attrition of CHVs working as village reporters (VRs) responsible for community-based death notification in the Malaria Vaccine Implementation Program (MVIP) in Malawi. METHODS: This mixed-methods exploratory study, which intersected with the case studies, was conducted from November 2022 to March 2023 in nine rural districts in southern and central Malawi. Purposive sampling was used to select 64 study participants for qualitative interviews. Using case studies, we conducted six in-depth interviews (IDIs) with CHVs who had dropped out, were reachable, and agreed to be interviewed-many were dispersed, hesitant to attend meetings, or unreachable for focus group discussions (FGDs). We held five FGDs (n = 50) with CHVs who remained in the MVIP for shared norms and experiences and eight key informant interviews (KIIs) with health workers, opinion leaders, and program staff to provide insights into health workers motivation, supervisory and program perspectives. Thematic analysis and the social capital framework (roles, relationships, and empowerment) were used to analyse and interpret the qualitative data. The qualitative study was complemented by a cross-sectional survey involving 696 randomly selected participants from a pool of 2,861 CVHs to demonstrate the trends of retention over time. Descriptive statistics were computed from quantitative survey data, with retention as a primary outcome (defined as whether a CHVs was willing to stay in the program). RESULTS: At the start of the program in 2019, a total of 2,861 CHVs were recruited by March 2023; only 295 (10.3%) had dropped out. Among 696 CHVs surveyed, the most commonly reported factors associated with retention were incentives (643; 92%), participation in exchange visits (377; 54%), and managing a small geographical area (275; 40%). Qualitative data from FGDs and KIIs corroborated these findings and identified compassion for serving others, financial and non‑financial incentives, and flexibility to work across multiple programmes as key motivators for continued participation. Factors associated with attrition included experiences of ridicule or disrespect, lack of opportunities for personal development, and limited career progression. IDIs with CHVs who left the programme provided in‑depth accounts of these individual‑level drivers, which helped explain patterns observed in the survey. CONCLUSION: Engagement of CHVs in community-based programs can be promoted by offering opportunities to serve others, incentives, and flexibility to work on multiple programmes. However, it is also important to address ridicule-making fun or rude comments and limited personal and career development, which act as barriers to the continued engagement of lay health workers.

title: Which aspects of restoration project organization relate to volunteer engagement in community‐based initiatives?
authors: Tim Alamenciak; Stephen D. Murphy
abstract: Abstract Introduction Project organization is an under‐studied but important aspect of volunteer engagement in ecological restoration and conservation. Previous studies on volunteer commitment have found that people are more engaged in well‐organized projects, but what constitutes good project organization from a volunteer perspective has not been empirically examined. Objectives This study investigates how the components of project organization (i.e. social capital, transformational leadership, and organizational capacity) relate to volunteer engagement in ecological restoration and conservation projects. Methods We conducted an online survey of volunteers in ecological restoration and conservation projects in Ontario, Canada (182 respondents accessed the survey; 143 provided analyzable responses) to examine the relationship between these three factors and volunteer engagement. Results A path analysis showed that transformational leadership ( β = 0.472, p < 0.001) and organizational capacity ( β = 0.263, p = 0.002) were positively associated with social capital, which in turn was positively associated with volunteer engagement ( β = 0.407, p < 0.001). The model accounted for 37.7% of the variance in social capital and 16.6% in volunteer engagement. Neither transformational leadership nor organizational capacity showed a direct association with volunteer engagement once social capital was accounted for. Conclusion Volunteer engagement was most strongly associated with social capital—the trust, shared vision, and interpersonal connections among volunteers—and the associations of leadership and organizational capacity with engagement appear to operate through it rather than independently. Because the design is cross‐sectional and single‐source, these are associations rather than causal effects. Practitioners seeking to increase engagement nonetheless have grounds to attend to the relational dimension of their programs alongside leadership and resourcing.

title: Dimensions of Culture and Experience of Support: A Cross-Cultural Comparison of Volunteers from Poland and Uganda
authors: Anna Kawula
abstract: Purpose: International non-governmental organizations operating in Sub-Saharan Africa, due to their nature and specific dynamics, play an important role in the local community by providing social support and assistance in resolving difficult situations without involving their governments.The aim of the study was to answer the following questions: (a) What cultural differences exist between volunteers from Poland and Uganda?(b) Do cultural values influence the experience of social support, and if so, how?The relationship between values, social capital, and support networks was examined.Design/Methodology/Approach: The study employs a cross-cultural comparative analysis based on empirical data collected from a sample of 136 volunteers, including students, teachers, and medical professionals from Poland and Uganda.Quantitative and qualitative data were examined to assess the interplay between cultural values, social capital, and social support networks.Findings: Analysis of the collected data reveals cultural differences in the perception of certain values (particularly attitudes toward time and success) and the relationship between these values and sociodemographic variables (community orientation), as well as the recognition of the negative consequences of the influence of Western values related to social capital.Practical Implications: The findings provide valuable insights for international nongovernmental organizations operating in Sub-Saharan Africa, enhancing their capacity to manage cross-cultural volunteer teams, optimizing social support networks, and mitigate the unintended negative consequences of introducing Western-centric values into local community structures.Originality/Value: This study fills a gap in the literature on the cross-cultural dynamics of volunteering between Central Europe (Poland) and East Africa (Uganda) by demonstrating how cultural dimensions, such as time perception and collectivism, transform social capital in developing regions.

title: Exploring the Nature and Forms of Women-Led Community Associations in Gbagyi Communities of the FCT
authors: Olufunke Grace Olabode; Emmanuel S. Dandaura; Daniel James Chikada
venue: African Journal of Stability and Development (AJSD)
abstract: This paper interrogates the developmental agency of women-led community associations as instruments of sustainable development among Gbagyi women in selected communities of the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja. The study is situated within the broader problematique of institutional deficit, wherein formal state apparatuses have proven inadequate in addressing the quotidian socio-economic precarities of rural and peri-urban populations. Notwithstanding the visibility of women’s collectives, Gbagyi women continue to grapple with entrenched poverty, financial exclusion, and epistemic marginalisation, thereby raising questions about the transformative capacity and long-term viability of these associations. Anchored in Participatory Development Theory and augmented by Social Capital Theory, the study adopts a convergent mixed-methods design. Primary data were generated from 370 validated questionnaire respondents and Focus Group Discussions across purposively selected Gbagyi settlements in Bwari, AMAC, and Kuje Area Councils. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative data underwent reflexive thematic analysis. Findings reveal that Rotational Savings and Credit Associations, cooperative societies, and faith-based fellowships constitute the predominant organisational modalities. These formations contribute substantively to income generation, financial resilience, and social cohesion. Their efficacy is, however, attenuated by chronic under-capitalisation, patriarchal cultural strictures, and the absence of formal institutional articulation with State structures. The paper concludes that women-led associations are not mere welfare appendages but legitimate grassroots governance institutions. It, therefore, recommends statutory recognition by the FCTA, gender-responsive empowerment programming by the Federal Ministry of Women Affairs, inclusive micro-finance architecture, and strategic collaboration with traditional authorities. Such measures are imperative to harness the associational capital of Gbagyi women for inclusive and sustainable development.

title: Differentiating Islamic values and their associations with Muslim community participation and rural community development
authors: Moh. Dulkiah; Ahmad Ali Nurdin; Akmaliyah Akmaliyah; Anggi Saeful Majid; Tri Adianto
abstract: This study examines how ukhuwah (brotherhood), amanah (trust and responsibility), and broader Islamic values influence Muslim community participation and rural community development in Indonesia. Using survey data from 693 Muslim middle-class respondents in rural areas of West Java, Central Java, and Yogyakarta, the study applies Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that Islamic values strongly influence Muslim community participation (β = 0.662, p < 0.001), while amanah has a small but significant effect (β = 0.074, p = 0.022). Ukhuwah has no significant effect (β = 0.037, p = 0.262). Muslim community participation strongly predicts community development (β = 0.729, p < 0.001) and mediates the effects of Islamic values and amanah on community development, but not that of ukhuwah . The model explains 53.2% of the variance in both participation and community development. The findings indicate that Islamic values do not function uniformly as drivers of rural development; their contribution depends on their translation into active community participation. The study extends faith-based social capital research by distinguishing the different roles of Islamic value dimensions in participatory rural development.
